calendarEvent.title: Fernhollow: duplicate jobs follow-up
calendarEvent.description:
Hi Owen,

Follow-up on the duplicate jobs issue (ticket #4817). Agenda:
1. Where the cleanup stands
2. What went wrong and what we changed
3. Next steps

Thanks,
Tom

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Hi Owen, thanks for making the time. Can you hear us okay?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, I can hear you. Sorry, I'm out by the truck yard, so it might get a bit noisy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: No worries at all. Shreyas is on as well, he's our CTO.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Lena sends her apologies, by the way. She's stuck on another customer call this afternoon.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No problem. Tell her I said hi.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Hi Owen. Thanks for jumping on. I know the last three weeks have been a real pain for your team.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's one way to put it. Look, I appreciate you both being here. I'll be honest, my dispatchers are pretty fed up, and so am I.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For about two weeks my two dispatch leads were spending an hour or two every morning just checking the board for jobs that shouldn't be there. That's time they're not spending on customers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But I'd rather spend this half hour on what happened and what changes, than on me venting at you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's fair, and honestly we want to hear the venting too if it helps. Maybe I'll start with where the cleanup stands, and then Shreyas can explain what actually went wrong.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sounds good, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, let me share my screen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can you see the spreadsheet? It should say Fernhollow duplicate cleanup at the top.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yep, I've got it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So, between the fifteenth of September and last Friday, the sync created a hundred and thirty-two duplicate jobs in your account. Every one of them is listed here, next to the original job it duplicated.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On Saturday morning we ran a cleanup script that Maya on our backend team wrote. It removed all one hundred and thirty-two duplicates and kept the original job in each pair.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And nothing real got deleted? That was my big worry. I don't want a tech showing up tomorrow morning and finding the job's just gone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Nothing real. We ran it in dry-run mode first, and I checked every pair by hand against the original booking.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The script only touches jobs that were created by the bad sync logic, and we kept a backup of everything it removed, just in case.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Good. That's a relief.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: One more thing on the cleanup you'll want to know. Two of the duplicates had been marked complete by a technician, so they ended up in your QuickBooks export on the twenty-eighth.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They're flagged in column F. Your customers didn't get billed twice as far as I can see, but the invoices exist in draft.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, that's useful. I'll get our billing person to void those two this week, before they go out with the month-end run.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now, the part I know matters most to you. Three of those duplicates were picked up by your auto-assign rule and given to a second technician, and those three jobs actually got dispatched twice.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's rows twelve, forty and ninety-one. The furnace service on Alder Road on the twenty-second, the water heater on Pine Street on the twenty-ninth, and the boiler check at the Brookside apartments on the first of October.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, I know those three very well. Two trucks rolled to each of them. On the Pine Street one the customer called our office asking why two plumbers were in her driveway.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's three wasted call-outs, about four hundred dollars each once you count the tech's time and the van. And honestly the embarrassment with the customer is worse than the money.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So I do want some kind of credit for that. I don't think that's unreasonable.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It's not unreasonable at all. I'd like to come back to that in a few minutes, because I want to make you an offer on this call rather than send it off into email.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. I'll hold you to that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Last thing on the cleanup. Since Saturday we haven't seen a single new duplicate. Maya put a temporary guard in on Friday night that blocks the bad case, and the proper fix goes out tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Tomorrow, so that's Tuesday?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Tuesday the sixth, yeah. I'll email you once it's deployed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Please do. Even a one-liner.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Will do. I'll send you this spreadsheet today too, with the three double dispatches highlighted. Okay, I'll stop sharing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So, what actually happened. I'll try to keep it plain, and stop me if anything doesn't make sense.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Your dispatchers book a lot of your maintenance contracts as recurring events. Quarterly furnace checks, annual boiler services, that kind of thing. And those sync into your technicians' Google calendars.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Right, that's most of our maintenance book. Several hundred recurring visits at this point.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: When someone moves just one visit in a series, say the October visit moves from Tuesday to Thursday, Google keeps it as part of the series but marks that one occurrence as an exception.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Our version one point four release, which went out on the fifteenth of September, changed how we match calendar events to jobs. And it stopped looking at the piece that says which occurrence of the series an event is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So every time a single visit was moved, we didn't recognise it as the same job. We thought it was brand new, and we created a second job for it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And then auto-assign handed the new one to whoever was free.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And on the technician's phone, the duplicate looked exactly like a real job? Same address, same notes, everything?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Exactly the same, apart from the job number. Which is why it was so hard for your techs to tell. From their side there was no way to know.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. A couple of my guys thought it was a second visit we'd booked on purpose, like a follow-up. One of them even called the customer to confirm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Exactly. Most of the time one of your dispatchers spotted the duplicate and deleted it. Three times, nobody did.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Why us, though? I was talking to a guy at another HVAC outfit who uses you, and he said he didn't see anything like this.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Because you move individual maintenance visits a lot more than most customers do. You have a big recurring book and your dispatchers reshuffle it constantly, which is completely normal for your business.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Other customers hit it a handful of times. You hit it a hundred and thirty-two times.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Great. Lucky us, then.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The honest part is that this should have been caught before it ever reached you. We didn't have a test for a moved occurrence of a recurring event.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We do now, and we're building a much bigger set of those tests into the next version of sync.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. I appreciate you saying that straight instead of dressing it up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So what's the fix, in plain English?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We now identify every calendar event by two things together, the event's ID and which occurrence of the series it is. So a moved visit is always recognised as the same job, just at a new time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And that's what goes out tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's what goes out tomorrow. Along with an alert on our side if the number of jobs sync creates for any one customer suddenly spikes, so we'd notice within hours instead of your team noticing after a week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That second part honestly matters more to me than the first. Things break, I get it. What bugs me is we were the ones who noticed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Agreed. That's the part I'm least happy about too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And while we're on it, when we first reported this on the twenty-third, it took a day and a half to get a real response. That didn't help my mood.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's on me, honestly. It got triaged as low priority because at first it looked like one technician's calendar acting up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And we've changed that. From now on, any ticket about duplicate or missing jobs is high priority by default, no matter how small it looks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Good. Because a missing job for us is a customer with no heat.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We're heading into the cold months now. October through February is when our phones don't stop. I can't have this happen in January.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Understood. That's exactly why the alerting matters. We'd rather find the next problem on a Tuesday afternoon than have your dispatchers find it on a Monday morning in January.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Will I get any of this in writing? My owner's going to ask me, and I'd much rather forward him something than try to explain occurrence IDs from memory.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes. You'll have a written postmortem from me by Friday the ninth. The timeline, the root cause, what we've changed, and what we're changing next.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I'll keep it to two pages and write it for someone who isn't an engineer. The technical appendix can go at the back for anyone who wants it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Two pages is about my owner's limit, so that's perfect.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Friday's fine, that works.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And if your owner wants to talk to me directly after he's read it, I'm happy to do that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'll let him know. He probably won't, though. He mostly cares about the money.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Which brings us to the credit. Here's what I'd like to do.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We'll credit you one full month of fees for all sixty of your technicians. At forty-five dollars a technician, that's two thousand seven hundred dollars, and it comes off your next invoice.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Does that include the three double dispatches? Or is that separate?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It's meant to cover everything, including those. Three call-outs at about four hundred each is twelve hundred, so this is more than double that, on purpose.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hmm. Let me think about that for a second.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Yeah, that's fair. I was going to ask for the twelve hundred and see what you said, so this is better than I expected, honestly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Good. Then let's call it agreed. Two thousand seven hundred dollars, on your November invoice. I'll confirm it in writing in the postmortem as well, so it's all in one place.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Perfect. Thank you for that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I'll make sure finance has it this week, so it doesn't get lost between now and November.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The other thing. And this is really the big one for me. We found out about this from our techs, not from you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I had a technician call me on the twenty-second asking why he had two jobs at the same house. That's how I learned you'd changed something.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I need a heads-up when you change anything about sync. I don't need to approve it, I just need to know, so my dispatchers can keep an eye out for a few days.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Completely fair. We do have a release notes email that goes out with every release. I'm pretty sure you were never on it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I've never seen it, no.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'll add you today. Do you want your dispatchers on it as well?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. Me and my two dispatch leads. I'll send you their emails after this call.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And on top of the general release notes, for anything that touches calendar sync specifically, we'll send you a notice forty-eight hours before it goes out. What's changing, and what to watch for.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Forty-eight hours is good. That gives us a working day to warn the techs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'll set that up on our side. Any release that touches sync gets a separate heads-up email to your list.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Could we go further and have some kind of test account? Like, a sandbox where we try the release before it hits our real schedule?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I'd love to say yes, but honestly, not this quarter. A proper sandbox with your real calendar data is a big piece of work, and I'd rather not promise it and then miss.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Fair enough. I'd rather you didn't promise it either.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Or, I mean, could we just stay on the old version of sync until we're ready to move?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We run one version for everyone, so pinning a customer to an old version isn't something we can do. The forty-eight hour notice is how we give you a chance to raise concerns before it ships.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Maybe we could look at a status page for sync at some point too, so you can see if something's off without having to email us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Maybe. Let's not commit to that one today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. So the email list, plus forty-eight hours for anything sync. That works for me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Who should the forty-eight hour notice go to? The same three people?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Same three. And maybe copy our office manager, she handles the customer calls when things go sideways. Actually, no, leave her off. I'll forward it if I need to.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Got it, just the three of you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: One request from our side. Could your dispatchers spot-check this week's schedule for anything that still looks duplicated? We're confident we got everything, but they know the book better than we do.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sure. I'll have them go through the week and I'll send you anything weird by Wednesday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Perfect, thank you, that helps.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Owen, is there anything else we haven't covered?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: One thing. When the next big sync change comes out, whatever that is, I'd want to know well ahead. Not forty-eight hours.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's fair. The next big one is Calendar Sync v2. It moves us from checking calendars every five minutes to Google and Microsoft telling us the moment something changes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Beta is in mid-November and general availability is early December.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Are we in the beta?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Only if you want to be. After the last three weeks I'd completely understand if you'd rather wait for the general release.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'd rather wait. Let somebody else find the bugs this time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Understood. You'll stay out of the beta, and you'll get the forty-eight hour notice before v2 reaches your account.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let me recap so we're all on the same page. I send you the cleanup spreadsheet with the three double dispatches marked, today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I add you and your two leads to the release notes list once you send me their emails, and I set up the forty-eight hour notice for sync changes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Shreyas sends the postmortem by Friday. The two thousand seven hundred dollar credit goes on your November invoice. And your team spot-checks the schedule and sends anything odd by Wednesday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And you email me when the fix is live tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And I email you when the fix is live tomorrow. Yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Thanks, both of you. I came into this pretty annoyed and I'm leaving a lot less annoyed. That's about as good as these calls get.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We'll take it. Thanks, Owen, and sorry again to you and the team.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Talk soon. Bye now.

decisions: Fernhollow receives a service credit of one month of fees for all sixty technicians ($2,700 at $45 per technician), applied to the November invoice, covering the three double dispatches.
Owen and his two dispatch leads are added to Deino's release-notes email list.
Deino will send Fernhollow a notice forty-eight hours before any release that touches calendar sync; the office manager is left off that list.
Shreyas will deliver a written postmortem to Fernhollow by Friday 9 October.
Fernhollow will not join the Calendar Sync v2 beta and will wait for general availability.
Any support ticket about duplicate or missing jobs is now high priority by default.

facts.question: How many duplicate jobs were removed from Fernhollow's account?
facts.answer: One hundred and thirty-two, created between 15 September and the previous Friday; the cleanup ran on Saturday morning.
facts.evidence: It removed all one hundred and thirty-two duplicates and kept the original job in each pair.

facts.question: How many jobs were dispatched twice, and which ones?
facts.answer: Three: the furnace service on Alder Road (22 Sept), the water heater on Pine Street (29 Sept) and the boiler check at the Brookside apartments (1 Oct).
facts.evidence: The furnace service on Alder Road on the twenty-second

facts.question: What did the double dispatches cost Fernhollow?
facts.answer: About four hundred dollars per wasted call-out, roughly twelve hundred dollars for the three.
facts.evidence: about four hundred dollars each once you count the tech's time and the van

facts.question: What caused the duplicate jobs?
facts.answer: The v1.4 release (15 September) changed event matching and stopped looking at which occurrence of a recurring series an event is, so a single moved occurrence was treated as a new event and a second job was created.
facts.evidence: And it stopped looking at the piece that says which occurrence of the series an event is.

facts.question: Why was Fernhollow hit harder than other customers?
facts.answer: Fernhollow books most maintenance as recurring events and its dispatchers move individual visits much more often than most customers.
facts.evidence: Because you move individual maintenance visits a lot more than most customers do.

facts.question: How big is the service credit and how was it calculated?
facts.answer: $2,700: one month of fees for sixty technicians at $45 per technician, applied to the November invoice.
facts.evidence: that's two thousand seven hundred dollars, and it comes off your next invoice

facts.question: When does the permanent fix go out?
facts.answer: Tuesday 6 October 2026; a temporary guard has been in place since Friday night.
facts.evidence: Maya put a temporary guard in on Friday night that blocks the bad case

facts.question: How much advance notice will Fernhollow get for sync changes?
facts.answer: Forty-eight hours before any release that touches calendar sync, on top of the general release-notes email.
facts.evidence: we'll send you a notice forty-eight hours before it goes out

facts.question: What additional monitoring is Deino adding?
facts.answer: An alert if the number of jobs sync creates for any one customer suddenly spikes, so Deino notices within hours.
facts.evidence: an alert on our side if the number of jobs sync creates for any one customer suddenly spikes

facts.question: Why can't Fernhollow stay on the old version of sync?
facts.answer: Deino runs one version for everyone, so pinning a customer to an old version is not possible; the 48-hour notice is the chance to raise concerns.
facts.evidence: so pinning a customer to an old version isn't something we can do

facts.question: Did any duplicate jobs reach Fernhollow's invoicing?
facts.answer: Two duplicates marked complete by a technician ended up as draft invoices in the QuickBooks export on 28 September; they are flagged in column F and Owen will have them voided.
facts.evidence: so they ended up in your QuickBooks export on the twenty-eighth
